questions.q: State what is meant by a standalone computer.

markPoints.concept: a computer that is not connected to a network
accept: not connected|no connection|not on a network|not networked|no network|on its own|by itself|alone|isolated|not linked
markPoints.exemplar: A computer that is not connected to a network.

questions.example: A computer that is not connected to any network.
questions.paraphrase: A machine working on its own, with no network connection.
questions.feedback: Not connected is the whole definition. Being portable or old has nothing to do with it.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 1 — Types of network: zoom out, station 1: Standalone computer

questions.q: Two standalone computers in the same room need to share a file. What has to happen?
options: The file has to be copied onto something and carried across
The file is sent automatically when both are switched on
One computer prints it and the other scans it back in
The file cannot be shared at all
questions.feedback: Without a network, the only route is physical. That inconvenience is the argument for networking.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 1 — Types of network: zoom out, station 1: Standalone computer

questions.q: Match each term to what it means.
pairs: A network over a small geographical area, on hardware the organisation owns
A network over a large geographical area, using connections the organisation does not own
questions.feedback: Size is the obvious difference; who owns the cable is the one that gets the marks.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 1 — Types of network: zoom out, station 11: Wide area network (WAN)

questions.q: Which of these is a wide area network?
options: A school's computer rooms, linked by its own switches
Two laptops sharing files over Bluetooth
A home router and the devices connected to it
questions.feedback: The internet is the largest WAN there is. The other three are all local.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 1 — Types of network: zoom out, station 11: Wide area network (WAN)

questions.q: Explain one difference between a LAN and a WAN, other than their size.

markPoints.concept: a LAN uses hardware the organisation owns
markPoints.exemplar: A LAN runs on hardware the organisation owns itself.

markPoints.concept: a WAN uses connections provided by someone else, such as a telecommunications company
markPoints.exemplar: A WAN uses connections rented from a telecommunications company.

questions.example: A LAN runs on cables and switches the organisation owns and looks after itself, while a WAN uses connections provided by a telecommunications company that the organisation rents rather than owns.
questions.paraphrase: With a local network the company owns all the equipment, whereas a wide area network relies on lines leased from an outside provider.
questions.feedback: Ownership of the connections. Saying only 'a WAN is bigger' is the size difference the question rules out.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 1 — Types of network: zoom out, station 11: Wide area network (WAN)

questions.q: A WAN is always slower than a LAN.
questions.feedback: False, though it usually is. A WAN crosses longer distances on connections shared with others, which normally means more latency — but a leased fibre WAN can be faster than an old LAN.
questions.misconception: 'WAN means slow' is a rule of thumb, not a definition.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 1 — Types of network: zoom out, station 11: Wide area network (WAN)

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it is an advantage or a disadvantage of networking a set of computers.
items: Files can be shared without copying them onto a drive
One printer can serve a whole room
Updates can be installed from one place
Malware can spread from one machine to all of them
If the server fails, nobody can work
Setting it up costs money and needs expertise
questions.feedback: Sharing is the advantage and the disadvantage: whatever can be shared includes the things you did not want shared.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 1 — Types of network: zoom out, station 8: Advantages

questions.q: A small business is deciding whether to network its six computers. Explain one disadvantage it should consider.

markPoints.concept: names a real disadvantage: cost, expertise, malware spreading, or a single point of failure
accept: server fail|server goes down|single point|everyone stops|nobody can|whole network|all of them stop
markPoints.exemplar: Malware on one computer could spread to all of them.

markPoints.concept: and explains what it would mean for this business
markPoints.exemplar: This means one infected machine could stop the whole business working.

questions.example: Malware is the main risk: on standalone machines an infection stays where it lands, but on a network it can spread to all six computers, so one careless download could stop the whole business working.
questions.paraphrase: If one machine picks up a virus it can travel to every other computer on the network, which means the entire business could be brought to a halt by a single infection.
questions.feedback: Name it, then say what it costs this business. The second mark is the application.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.3 Lesson 1 — Types of network: zoom out, station 8: Advantages
